title: Holi: love without a body
hookLine: Shiva's third eye burns the god of love to ash, and love lives on without a body
carry: kama: love is an aim of life, within dharma
last: SATYA: THE DOOR OPENED FOR TRUTH, NOT BIRTH.

cards: Shiva sits in meditation on a mountain, so deep and so still that nothing reaches him. He's been there since his first wife, Sati, died. The gods need him to wake up, to marry again, to have a son who can defeat a demon.

So they send the god of love, Kama, with his bow of sugarcane and his arrows of flowers, to shoot one into Shiva's heart. You've met Prahlad walking out of the fire, and Krishna coloring Radha's face in Braj.
This is Holi's third story, and in parts of south India it's the one told at Holi's full moon.

teach.b: Kama shoots. The arrow lands. And Shiva opens his third eye.
Fire pours out of it, and Kama is burned to ash where he stands. His wife, Rati, falls weeping on the ashes. Here the story turns.
Shiva, moved, promises that Kama will live again, but without a body. Love, from now on, will be everywhere and visible nowhere. That's why one of Kama's names is Ananga, the bodiless one.

And Shiva does wake, and does marry Parvati. In parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, Holi's full moon is remembered as Kama Dahanam, the burning of Kama, with fires and songs of Rati's grief. Now the teaching.
You might expect a god of ascetics to end love for good. The tradition doesn't.

teach.h: FOUR AIMS OF A HUMAN LIFE.
teach.b: Kama, love, desire and enjoyment, is one of the four aims of a human life that Hinduism names: dharma, doing right; artha, making a living; kama, love and pleasure; and moksha, freedom. Love isn't the enemy.
It's one of the goals. But it isn't the boss, either.
Kama is meant to be held inside dharma.

teach.h: LOVE IS AN AIM OF LIFE.
teach.b: Many teachers read Shiva's fire that way: love that barges in uninvited gets burned, and love that serves the right thing, here a marriage the whole world needed, is given back and set loose everywhere.
Then comes Holi morning, and the colors. And that's the last of the stories, for now. Tomorrow the path turns to practice: breath, mantra, a home shrine.
The stories come with you. Kama: love is an aim of life, within dharma.

how: In parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, the Holi full moon is kept as Kama Dahanam, remembering Kama burned by Shiva's third eye, with bonfires and songs; across India, the day after the full moon is kept with colors.

games.q: a friend says: 'Shiva burned the god of love, so Hinduism must be against love.' what's the best answer?
o: right. real Hindus give up every desire.
no: Kama lives on without a body, and kama is one of the four aims of life, inside dharma.
it's just a myth, so it doesn't say anything.
games.why: Shiva didn't end love; he set it loose. the tradition names kama, love and enjoyment, as an aim of life, held within dharma.

practice: Bring to mind a love in your life: a person, a place, something you enjoy. In Hindu teaching it's nothing to be ashamed of; it's one of life's aims.

Now ask it one honest question: does this love sit inside doing right, or is it pushing dharma out of the way? If you pray, offer that love to God and ask that it serve what's right. Then breathe, and let yourself be glad of it.

wordCard.voice: Holi. The festival of colors, the morning after the fire, where Prahlad, Radha and Kama all have a story.

orig.note: Sanskrit: without a body, a name for Kama after Shiva's fire.

carryVoice: Your line: kama: love is an aim of life, within dharma. Love got loose in the world. That's the last of the stories, for now.
